rv.q: The intimacy of the Golden Theatre keeps us close to these men for more than two hours, and watching them is thrilling.
It's a time bomb that will always be ready to detonate.

Parks' 'Topdog/Underdog' is a phenomenal two-brother drama, every bit as intense and rich as anything by Sam Shepard and, frankly, as good an American play as most anything written during the last quarter century.

Under the direction of Kenny Leon — a longtime Broadway hand here masterminding the best production of his career — the fierce rivalry and protectiveness binding this Lincoln and Booth convulses in a shattering denouement.
Give all credit to the playwright, the director and this cast that when fate comes calling in this fine revival of a 20-year-old play, it’ll still steal your breath away.
How wonderful to experience again, in the hilarious, harrowing and superbly acted Broadway revival that opened on Thursday at the Golden Theater, Parks’s fearlessness.
Director Kenny Leon has helmed a sharp, focused revival of the 2002 drama, with a pair of cracking performances that never let up.
America won’t let these men out; Emancipation won’t let these men out; the grim, violent preoccupation with male potency won’t let these men out.
The latest revival of the Pulitzer-prize winning two-hander is hysterical, tragic and above all sincere.
Hawkins and Abdul-Mateen shine as bright as Parks could ever dream.
The confidence radiating from both performances keeps Topdog/Underdog, a play with a winking eagerness to elude meaning, light, electric and most of all funny.
The production benefits immeasurably from two superb performances by Corey Hawkins and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II.
I suppose we shouldn’t be surprised that this play had another card up its sleeve.
Indeed, the play’s inexorable march to tragedy, which some critics have tagged as melodramatic or unearned, lands a bit differently now, and sticks harder in the craw, than it did 20 years ago.
The dialogue between the two men positively crackles throughout, and the interplay between Abdul-Mateen and Hawkins—both edgy, raw, hilarious, and real—is razor-sharp.
With her spectacularly vivid dialogue that sails across the boards and over the audience, she holds us spellbound in one room with two men and a world of life and story.
More than anything, this play is a showcase for the writing and the acting, and it's a brilliant success by both measures.
Suzan-Lori Parks’ Topdog/Underdog (Golden Theatre, to January 15), directed by Kenny Leon, is a brilliant, electrifying piece of theater for many reasons.
Every element in Kenny Leon’s hilarious, harrowing new revival, from the casting to the design, conspires to leave you shaken and stirred, and exuberantly entertained.
Kenny Leon's mesmerizing and exquisitely acted revival
Susan-Lori Parks’ Topdog/Underdog handles this beautifully and never lets attention flag for a moment.
In this starry and stirring revival, the play unfurls in all its glory.
Every moment is filled with dialog and actions that convey layers of meaning with every word, every joke, every gesture, every bit of sexual boasting and competitiveness.
Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Corey Hawkins give powerhouse performances in this riveting revival

Regardless, the production excels in the sharp and textured interplay between Abdul-Mateen (restless, longing, cocky, hurt) and Hawkins (weathered, mature, guilty, smooth), in which comedy-laced routines eventually culminate in showdown and tragedy.
There’s too much of a deluxe air to this production that ultimately sinks its ambitions to be anything close to the definitive version of Parks’ writing, which remains stellar.

The anachronism of the card game is not all that felt dated about this “Topdog/Underdog…[hile Kenny Leon’s direction highlights some comic moments and drives home some poignant ones – and Lord knows neither American violence nor Black despair are out-of-date — there is little in the current production that feels urgent.
Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Corey Hawkins bring a raw, electric energy to Suzan-Lori Parks's Pulitzer Prize-winning play that makes this revival feel urgent and vital.
Both actors display an impressive physicality, commanding attention in long dialog-free scenes and circling each other in the cramped bed-sit like wary prizefighters on the senior circuit.
The two actors dominate, taking full control of the energy and tensions around them.
The play is beautifully crafted and the characters deftly drawn.
But it’s all on one note, on one level of emotion and action.

cn.t: Parks' Pulitzer winner crackles with electricity in this vital 20th anniversary revival, powered by phenomenal performances from Hawkins and Abdul-Mateen II that breathe urgent new life into the tale of brotherly rivalry.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
